title: Acetaminophen Poisoning: Time, Level, NAC, and the New Canadian Protocol
bottomLine: Potentially toxic acetaminophen exposure requires a reliable ingestion history, timed serum acetaminophen concentration when the nomogram applies, liver testing and early N-acetylcysteine when indicated. Canadian poison centres adopted a revised IV NAC protocol in 2026, so outdated infusion schedules should not be memorized as universal.
recognize: Early symptoms may be absent or mild despite potentially severe later hepatotoxicity; repeated supratherapeutic ingestion is assessed differently from a single acute timed ingestion.
differentiate: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram is for a single acute ingestion with a known time and should not be applied to repeated, staggered or unknown-time exposures.
assessment: Identify all acetaminophen-containing products, amount, formulation, time, repeated dosing, body weight, co-ingestants, fasting or liver risk and suicidal intent.
workup: Obtain serum acetaminophen at the appropriate time, AST/ALT, INR and chemistry according to exposure pattern; consult a Canadian poison centre for complex or delayed presentations.
management: Start NAC when indicated and do not delay it in a high-risk late or uncertain presentation while awaiting nonessential results; use the current regional Canadian poison-centre protocol and stopping criteria.
medicationSafety: A revised two-step IV NAC protocol aligned with Canadian poison-centre standards launched in Ontario in April 2026; local poison-centre guidance is the source of truth for dosing and continuation.
counselling: After recovery, reconcile all OTC combination products and address intentional-poisoning safety needs.
followUp: Continue NAC and monitoring until poison-centre or protocol stopping criteria are met; transfer liver failure promptly.
examTrap: Using the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for repeated supratherapeutic dosing over several days.
oneLinePearl: The acetaminophen nomogram only works when the ingestion pattern fits the nomogram.
sourceBasis: Ontario Poison Centre patient care resources and revised 2026 IV NAC protocol
Canadian Association for Poison Centres and Clinical Toxicology

title: Salicylate Poisoning: Tachypnea Is Compensation, Not Reassurance
bottomLine: Salicylate poisoning causes mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis and can worsen despite a falling serum concentration. Avoid suppressing compensatory hyperventilation; alkalinization and dialysis decisions depend on symptoms, acid-base status, renal function and level trends.
recognize: Tinnitus, vomiting, tachypnea, diaphoresis, fever, confusion and acid-base disturbance are classic.
differentiate: Sepsis, DKA and stimulant toxicity can produce tachypnea and acidosis; chronic salicylate toxicity can occur at lower concentrations in older adults.
assessment: Ask product, dose, timing, chronic use, renal disease and co-ingestants; assess mental status, respiratory effort and volume status.
workup: Trend salicylate levels, blood gas, electrolytes, glucose and renal function; a single level may be misleading when absorption is delayed.
management: Correct volume and potassium deficits, use sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize serum and urine when indicated, and involve poison centre/nephrology early for severe toxicity or dialysis criteria.
medicationSafety: Intubation can precipitate sudden deterioration if adequate minute ventilation and alkalemia are not maintained; it is a high-risk procedure in severe salicylism.
counselling: Review hidden aspirin/salicylate products after accidental chronic toxicity.
followUp: Continue serial levels until clearly falling with clinical improvement.
examTrap: Intubating a compensating salicylate-poisoned patient and allowing the PaCO2 to rise to a normal range.
oneLinePearl: In salicylate toxicity, hyperventilation is lifesaving compensation.
sourceBasis: Ontario Poison Centre salicylate urine-alkalinization resource

title: Toxic Alcohols: Think Osmol Gap Early, Anion Gap Later
bottomLine: Methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning can initially present with inebriation and an osmol gap, then evolve to severe anion-gap acidosis as toxic metabolites accumulate. Start antidotal therapy when suspicion is high rather than waiting for a send-out level in a deteriorating patient.
recognize: Methanol can cause visual symptoms; ethylene glycol can cause renal injury and hypocalcemia, but early symptoms are often nonspecific.
differentiate: Isopropanol causes ketosis without the same high-anion-gap acidosis and is managed differently.
assessment: Ask access to windshield washer fluid, antifreeze, solvents or intentional ingestion; assess vision, CNS status, breathing and renal symptoms.
workup: Calculate anion and osmol gaps, obtain blood gas, electrolytes, renal function and toxic alcohol levels when available; gaps change over time and neither alone excludes poisoning.
management: Give fomepizole when criteria or strong suspicion are met and involve poison centre/nephrology for hemodialysis decisions and adjunctive therapy.
medicationSafety: Do not delay fomepizole for confirmatory toxic-alcohol concentration when severe exposure is strongly suspected and testing is delayed.
counselling: After accidental exposure, emphasize original-container storage and poison-centre access.
followUp: Monitor acid-base and organ injury until metabolite formation and exposure risk have resolved.
examTrap: Ruling out toxic alcohol because the osmol gap is normal late in the presentation despite severe anion-gap acidosis.
oneLinePearl: The osmol gap can disappear as the dangerous anion gap appears.
sourceBasis: Ontario Poison Centre antidote stocking guidance 2026

title: Carbon Monoxide: Pulse Oximetry Can Look Normal
bottomLine: Carbon monoxide poisoning should be considered when multiple people from the same environment develop headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion or collapse. Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin and can appear reassuringly normal.
recognize: Exposure sources include faulty combustion appliances, fires, engines and enclosed-space generators; pregnancy creates fetal risk even when maternal symptoms are modest.
differentiate: Viral illness, migraine and food poisoning can mimic household clusters, but the shared environmental pattern is the clue.
assessment: Remove from exposure, assess airway/breathing/circulation, neurologic status, chest pain, pregnancy and fire/smoke co-exposure.
workup: Measure carboxyhemoglobin with co-oximetry and assess ECG/troponin, lactate or cyanide risk based on severity; level may fall after oxygen and does not perfectly correlate with symptoms.
management: Give high-concentration oxygen promptly and consult poison centre/hyperbaric specialists for severe neurologic, cardiac, pregnancy or other high-risk features.
medicationSafety: Do not use a normal SpO2 to decide oxygen is unnecessary.
counselling: Do not return to the exposure environment until the source has been assessed and corrected.
followUp: Provide return precautions for delayed neurocognitive symptoms after significant exposure.
examTrap: Ruling out carbon monoxide poisoning because pulse oximetry reads 99%.
oneLinePearl: A normal pulse oximeter does not rule out carbon monoxide.
sourceBasis: Canadian poison-centre and emergency medicine practice resources

title: Serotonin Syndrome vs NMS: Clonus or Rigidity?
bottomLine: Serotonin toxicity develops rapidly after serotonergic exposure and is characterized by neuromuscular hyperactivity such as clonus and hyperreflexia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome usually evolves more slowly with severe rigidity and dopamine blockade. Both require culprit-drug cessation and aggressive supportive care.
recognize: Serotonin syndrome: agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, diarrhea, clonus/hyperreflexia. NMS: hyperthermia, autonomic instability, altered mental status and lead-pipe rigidity with elevated CK.
differentiate: Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin and urinary retention rather than diaphoresis/clonus; malignant hyperthermia is peri-anesthetic.
assessment: Review all prescriptions, OTC cough products, supplements, illicit drugs, recent dose changes and antipsychotic/dopamine-withdrawal exposures.
workup: Use CK, renal function, electrolytes, ECG and cause-specific testing for complications; diagnosis is clinical.
management: Stop offending agents, cool and support ABCs; use benzodiazepines for agitation and specialty-directed antidotal or dopamine-restoring therapy when indicated.
medicationSafety: Multiple serotonergic agents and MAOI interactions can produce severe toxicity; do not restart culprit therapy until appropriately reassessed.
counselling: Teach patients to include OTC and herbal products in medication reconciliation.
followUp: Document culprit combinations and safe future alternatives.
examTrap: Calling any fever in a patient taking an SSRI serotonin syndrome without checking for clonus/hyperreflexia and competing causes.
oneLinePearl: Serotonin toxicity is a neuromuscular exam diagnosis.

title: Hypertensive Emergency: Treat Organ Injury, Not the Number Alone
bottomLine: Hypertensive emergency is severe blood-pressure elevation with acute target-organ injury such as encephalopathy, aortic syndrome, ACS, pulmonary edema or AKI. Severe asymptomatic hypertension is not the same syndrome and should not be rapidly normalized with IV therapy.
recognize: Headache alone does not define hypertensive emergency; organ injury does.
differentiate: Preeclampsia/eclampsia is a pregnancy-specific hypertensive emergency; aortic dissection requires a different hemodynamic strategy from ischemic stroke.
assessment: Repeat BP with correct technique and assess neurologic, cardiac, aortic, renal, retinal and pregnancy-related symptoms.
workup: Use ECG, creatinine/urinalysis, troponin, chest or neurovascular imaging and pregnancy-specific testing according to suspected organ injury.
management: Use monitored IV antihypertensive treatment with syndrome-specific rate and target of reduction; manage the target-organ emergency concurrently.
For severe BP without acute organ injury, adjust chronic therapy and arrange prompt follow-up rather than reflexively using IV medication.
medicationSafety: Overly rapid BP reduction can cause cerebral, coronary or renal ischemia; targets differ in aortic dissection, stroke and pregnancy.
counselling: Explain that long-term BP control and acute emergency BP lowering are different treatment problems.
followUp: After stabilization, confirm chronic hypertension treatment using current 2025 Canadian thresholds and out-of-office assessment when appropriate.
examTrap: Giving IV antihypertensive medication to rapidly normalize a very high BP in an asymptomatic patient with no acute organ injury.
oneLinePearl: The emergency is injured organs, not a frightening BP number by itself.
sourceBasis: Hypertension Canada guidelines and hypertensive emergency principles

title: Heat Illness: CNS Dysfunction Means Heat Stroke
bottomLine: Heat stroke is hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction and is a cooling emergency. Do not wait for laboratory confirmation; rapid active cooling and supportive care are time-critical.
recognize: Heat exhaustion causes weakness, nausea, dizziness and volume depletion without major CNS dysfunction; heat stroke causes confusion, seizure, delirium or coma.
differentiate: Sepsis, serotonin syndrome, NMS, anticholinergic toxicity and thyroid storm can cause hyperthermia.
assessment: Measure core temperature when possible and assess CNS, hydration, medications, exertion, environmental exposure and comorbidities.
workup: Use electrolytes, renal/liver tests, CK, coagulation and ECG in significant heat illness to identify organ injury.
management: Begin rapid active cooling immediately while supporting ABCs; cold-water immersion is highly effective for exertional heat stroke where feasible, while evaporative or other active cooling may be used according to setting.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics do not treat heat stroke because the hypothalamic set point is not the problem.
counselling: Review hydration, acclimatization, medications and heat-warning plans for vulnerable patients.
followUp: Severe heat stroke requires organ-function follow-up and graded return to exertion.
examTrap: Giving acetaminophen for heat stroke while delaying active cooling.
oneLinePearl: Heat stroke is cooled, not antipyreticked.

title: Hypothermia and Frostbite: Rewarm the Core, Protect Frozen Tissue
bottomLine: Hypothermia slows metabolism and makes the myocardium irritable; handle severe cases gently, remove wet clothing and rewarm according to severity. Frostbitten tissue should be rapidly rewarmed only when refreezing can be prevented.
recognize: Shivering may disappear in severe hypothermia; altered consciousness, bradycardia and slow respirations can be profound without indicating death.
differentiate: Cold diuresis, hypoglycemia, intoxication and trauma can coexist and worsen hypothermia.
assessment: Measure core temperature when possible, assess glucose, trauma, exposure duration, wetness, circulation and frozen tissue.
workup: Use ECG, electrolytes, glucose, blood gas and organ testing for moderate/severe cases.
management: Use passive external warming for mild cases and active external/core rewarming for more severe disease; perform frostbite rewarming in circulating warm water when refreezing is not possible and seek burn/vascular expertise for severe injury.
medicationSafety: Avoid rubbing or dry heat on frostbitten tissue; medication metabolism may be altered in severe hypothermia.
counselling: Address housing, occupational and substance-use factors that contributed to exposure.
followUp: Severe frostbite requires specialty follow-up for tissue viability and neuropathic sequelae.
examTrap: Thawing a foot in the field when the patient must still walk through freezing conditions and the tissue will refreeze.
oneLinePearl: Do not thaw frostbite until you can keep it thawed.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency and wilderness medicine practice resources

title: Burns: Stop the Burning, Size the Injury, Protect the Airway
bottomLine: Burn care starts with scene safety, stopping the burning process and ABCs. Depth, total body surface area, location, inhalation/electrical/chemical mechanism and age/comorbidity determine fluid, referral and airway needs.
recognize: Facial burns, soot, hoarseness, enclosed-space fire and progressive airway swelling raise inhalation concern; electrical burns may hide deep tissue injury.
differentiate: Superficial erythema is not counted in resuscitation TBSA; children have different body-surface proportions.
assessment: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, carbon monoxide exposure, burn depth/TBSA, circumferential injury, pain and associated trauma.
workup: Use carboxyhemoglobin, ECG/CK/renal tests for appropriate inhalation/electrical injuries and pregnancy testing where relevant to imaging/treatment.
management: Cool with cool running water early when appropriate but avoid ice/hypothermia, cover wounds, provide analgesia, update tetanus and use weight/TBSA-guided resuscitation for major burns with burn-centre consultation.
medicationSafety: Do not use ice directly on significant burns; topical antibiotics are wound-specific and not a substitute for burn assessment.
counselling: Teach wound care and infection signs for minor burns managed outpatient.
followUp: Burn depth evolves; reassess deeper or uncertain injuries and refer when healing trajectory is poor.
examTrap: Applying ice directly to a large thermal burn and causing further tissue injury and hypothermia.
oneLinePearl: Major burn care is airway and physiology before it is dressings.
sourceBasis: Canadian burn and emergency care principles

title: Trauma: Primary Survey Before the Perfect History
bottomLine: Major trauma is managed by immediate life threats in an ABCDE sequence while hemorrhage control and team activation occur in parallel. A complete history and definitive diagnosis come after airway, breathing and circulation threats are addressed.
recognize: Occult hemorrhage can be present despite initially normal BP, especially in young patients; older adults and beta-blocked patients may lack tachycardia.
differentiate: Shock mechanism can be hemorrhagic, obstructive, neurogenic or cardiogenic after trauma.
assessment: Perform airway with cervical-spine protection, breathing/chest threats, circulation and external hemorrhage, disability/GCS and exposure while preventing hypothermia.
workup: Use focused ultrasound, x-ray and CT according to stability; an unstable patient with an obvious surgical bleeding source should not be delayed in CT.
management: Control hemorrhage, use blood products and tranexamic acid when indicated, decompress tension pneumothorax and move rapidly to definitive trauma/surgical care.
medicationSafety: Excess crystalloid can worsen dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia in major hemorrhage.
counselling: Family communication occurs without delaying resuscitation and should be honest about evolving uncertainty.
followUp: After stabilization, complete secondary survey and re-examine because injuries are commonly missed during initial resuscitation.
examTrap: Sending a hemodynamically unstable trauma patient to CT before controlling an obvious life-threatening hemorrhage.
oneLinePearl: In trauma, physiology decides the next room.
sourceBasis: Canadian trauma care and ATLS-compatible principles

title: Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle Breakdown Can Become Kidney Failure
bottomLine: Rhabdomyolysis is muscle injury with CK elevation and risk of hyperkalemia, AKI and compartment syndrome. Treat the cause, restore appropriate volume and monitor electrolytes and renal function rather than relying on urine colour alone.
recognize: Triggers include crush injury, prolonged immobilization, seizures, extreme exertion, hyperthermia, statin interactions and toxins.
differentiate: Dark urine may be hematuria or bilirubin; urine dip positive for blood with few/no RBCs supports myoglobinuria.
assessment: Assess muscle pain/weakness, compartment symptoms, urine output, heat/exertion, medications, substances and immobilization.
workup: Trend CK, potassium, calcium/phosphate, creatinine, urinalysis and ECG when electrolyte risk is significant.
management: Use isotonic IV fluids tailored to volume status and urine output, stop the trigger and urgently treat hyperkalemia or compartment syndrome.
medicationSafety: Review statin-drug interactions and nephrotoxins; routine bicarbonate or mannitol is not universally indicated.
counselling: For exertional cases, give a graded return and hydration/heat plan after recovery.
followUp: Recheck renal function and CK until clearly resolving.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because their urine is not dark despite severe muscle pain and a very high CK after heat injury.
oneLinePearl: Rhabdomyolysis is a CK-and-kidney problem, not a cola-urine requirement.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency and nephrology practice resources

title: Unknown Poisoning: Toxidrome, ABCs, ECG, Glucose, Poison Centre
bottomLine: When the substance is unknown, stabilize first and use toxidromes, ECG, glucose, temperature, pupils, skin, bowel sounds and medication access to narrow the cause. Contact a Canadian poison centre early rather than relying on broad urine drug screens.
recognize: Opioid, sympathomimetic, anticholinergic, cholinergic and sedative-hypnotic toxidromes create recognizable physiologic patterns.
differentiate: A positive urine drug screen may represent remote exposure and can miss clinically important substances; it does not replace the bedside syndrome.
assessment: Assess ABCs, glucose, vitals, temperature, pupils, skin, secretions, bowel/bladder, neuromuscular exam, trauma and access to medications/chemicals.
workup: ECG is essential for many cardiotoxic ingestions; obtain acetaminophen concentration in important intentional/unknown ingestions and use targeted levels/tests based on syndrome.
management: Provide supportive care and syndrome-specific antidotes when indicated; consult the regional poison centre for exposure-specific treatment and observation.
medicationSafety: Activated charcoal is not routine for every ingestion and requires appropriate timing, substance and protected airway.
counselling: After intentional ingestion, complete psychiatric and means-safety assessment before disposition.
followUp: Observation duration depends on formulation, toxicokinetics and clinical course, not a fixed universal number of hours.
examTrap: Using a negative urine drug screen to declare an unconscious patient has not been poisoned.
oneLinePearl: The toxidrome and ECG are often more useful than the drug screen.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for Poison Centres and Clinical Toxicology

title: Refractory Anaphylaxis: Repeat Epinephrine and Escalate the Airway-Circulation Plan
bottomLine: IM epinephrine is first-line anaphylaxis treatment and should be repeated when response is inadequate while airway, oxygenation, IV fluids and emergency support escalate. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts, not rescue therapy.
recognize: Anaphylaxis can occur without skin findings and can present with hypotension, bronchospasm, upper-airway swelling or severe GI symptoms after a likely trigger.
differentiate: Vasovagal reaction causes bradycardia/pallor rather than bronchospasm or urticaria; panic does not cause objective airway edema or shock.
assessment: Assess airway voice/stridor, breathing, BP/perfusion, skin, GI symptoms, trigger and beta-blocker use.
workup: Do not delay epinephrine for tryptase; serum tryptase can support later investigation in selected cases.
management: Give IM epinephrine promptly and repeat as needed, position appropriately, give oxygen and IV crystalloid for shock, and use advanced infusion/airway protocols with experienced emergency care for refractory disease.
medicationSafety: There is no absolute contraindication to IM epinephrine in true anaphylaxis; IV bolus epinephrine outside appropriate resuscitation expertise can be dangerous.
counselling: Before discharge, prescribe/teach auto-injector use when indicated and provide allergist referral and trigger-avoidance plan.
followUp: Observation is individualized to severity and recurrence risk; biphasic reactions are possible.
examTrap: Giving an antihistamine first because the patient has hives while their BP is falling.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology anaphylaxis resources
